Hierarchical clustering and aggregation for multivariate GLM exponential-family data

Source: R/glm_cluster.R
glm_cluster.Rd

glm_cluster() performs Ward hierarchical clustering on a deviance (Jensen-Shannon divergence) dissimilarity matrix from glm_dist, adaptively cuts the dendrogram using (dynamicTreeCut), and then calls glm_aggregate() to aggregate columns belonging to the same cluster.

glm_aggregate() can also be called directly when you already have a vector of cluster memberships and want to reuse it across multiple datasets.

This function can be used for clustering or as a feature-grouping dimensionality-reduction technique for multivariate GLM data conforming to any exponential-family distribution (e.g. Poisson, Binomial, Gaussian, Gamma, Inverse-Gaussian). For aggregation, we use summation for count families and weighted or unweighted means for the other distributions.

Applications, among others, include grouping correlated mass traces in GC/MS datasets or clustering genes with correlated gene-expression patterns in RNA-seq datasets.

Usage

glm_cluster(
  Y,
  weights = NULL,
  family = poisson(identity),
  method = if (family$family == "poisson") "poissondist" else "deviance",
  size_fac = colSums(Y),
  rowbins = 1L
)

glm_aggregate(Y, weights = NULL, family = poisson(identity), clusterids)

Arguments

Y

A numeric matrix (`nrow(Y)` observations x `ncol(Y)` variables). Sparse `Matrix::dgCMatrix` is accepted. Proportion data should be provided in case of binomial data.

weights

Optional `nrow(Y) x ncol(Y)` matrix of precision weights (e.g. total counts for Binomial, `1/var` for Gaussian). Only used with `method = "deviance"`.

family

A **stats** family object (default `poisson(identity)`).

method

`"deviance"` or `"poissondist"` (default for family `poisson(identity)`).

size_fac

Size factors used for method `"poissondist"` (default colSums(Y), should be changed to rowSums(Y) if t(Y) is analysed to cluster rows rather than columns).

rowbins

Positive integer. If rowbins > 1 the function first aggregates every rowbins successive rows (time points, samples) to speed up distance computation and clustering; clusters are inferred on the binned matrix, but the final Y_agg is computed from the original (unbinned) data. Default rowbins = 1 skips this step.

clusterids

Integer vector of cluster labels (length = ncol(Y)); required by glm_aggregate(), returned by glm_cluster().

Value

A list

D

dist object returned by glm_dist()

hc

hclust object (using method Ward.D)

clusterids

integer vector with cluster ID memberships returned by cutreeDynamic()

Y_agg

matrix with per-cluster aggregated columns (summed for poisson and binomial, averaged within clusters for the other families)

weights_agg

aggregated weights (NULL if weights=NULL)

Details

Clustering via Ward's minimisation of within-cluster deviance, using the \(\sqrt{\mathrm{JS}}\) divergence, is a special case of agglomerative Bregman clustering (Telgarsky & Dasgupta 2012); the Jensen-Shannon divergence is itself a Bregman divergence for exponential-family log-likelihoods (Banerjee et al. 2005). Because \(\sqrt{\mathrm{JS}}\) is a true metric (Endres & Schindelin 2003), Ward linkage yields monotone dendrograms (see Nielsen 2016, Example 3). The dendrogram height equals the cumulative increase in cluster Bregman information.

Distance formulas used internally (see glm_dist)
For two columns i and j we write \(y_{ti}\), \(y_{tj}\) for their values at row t and \(w_{ti}\), \(w_{tj}\) for optional precision weights.

  • Symmetrised unit deviance (method = "deviance", default)
    $$ D_{ij}^{\text{dev}} \;=\; \sum_t \Bigl[ d\!\bigl(y_{ti},\;\bar\mu_t,\;w_{ti}\bigr) \;+\; d\!\bigl(y_{tj},\;\bar\mu_t,\;w_{tj}\bigr) \Bigr], \qquad \bar\mu_t \;=\; \frac{w_{ti}y_{ti}+w_{tj}y_{tj}}{w_{ti}+w_{tj}}, $$ where \(d(y,\mu,w)\) is the unit deviance returned by family$dev.resids(y, mu, w). For the Gaussian(identity) family \(d(y,\mu,w)=w(y-\mu)^2\), hence \(D_{ij}^{\text{dev}}=\tfrac12\sum_t w_t(y_{ti}-y_{tj})^2\) - exactly one-half the (weighted) squared Euclidean distance, so \(\sqrt{\mathrm{JS}}\) is Euclidean up to the constant \(\sqrt{1/2}\).

  • Poisson size-factor distance (Witten 2011) (method = "poissondist")
    With column size factors \(s_i\), row totals \(c_t=y_{ti}+y_{tj}\) and smoothing \(\beta\) (default 1): $$ n_{ti}= \frac{s_i\,c_t}{s_i+s_j}, \qquad d_i = \frac{y_{ti}+\beta}{n_{ti}+\beta} $$ $$ D_{ij}^{\mathrm{pois}} = \sum_t \Bigl[ n_{ti}+n_{tj} - n_{ti}d_i-n_{tj}d_j + y_{ti}\log d_i + y_{tj}\log d_j \Bigr]. $$

Both expressions equal twice the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the empirical distributions of columns i and j; taking the square-root gives a proper metric. Ward's linkage then minimises the increase in within-cluster Bregman information (see Telgarsky & Dasgupta 2012).

Note that hierarchical clustering is feasible only for moderately large data sets; for very large matrices more scalable Bregman k-means/X-means alternatives could be considered (Banerjee et al. 2005).

Functions

  • glm_aggregate(): Aggregate columns of \(Y\) over given cluster IDs.

References

Telgarsky, M. & Dasgupta, S. (2012). Agglomerative Bregman Clustering. Proceedings of the 29th International Conference on Machine Learning, 59-66.
Banerjee, A., Merugu, S., Dhillon, I., & Ghosh, J. (2005). Clustering with Bregman Divergences. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 6, 1705-1749.
Endres, D. M. & Schindelin, J. E. (2003). A New Metric for Probability Distributions. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 49(7), 1858-1860.
Hierarchical Clustering. In: Nielsen, F., Barbaresco, F. (eds.) Geometric Theory of Information, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 10589, pp. 369-395. Springer, Cham. doi:10.1007/978-3-319-21903-5_8
Witten, D. M. (2011). Classification and Clustering of Sequencing Data using a Poisson Model. Annals of Applied Statistics 5(4): 2493-2518.

Examples

# \donttest{
data(GCMS_data2)                        # GC/MS beer-volatile window
Y <- GCMS_data2                         # 1764 scans x 518 m/z traces

##--- 1. Ward-Bregman clustering with Poisson size-factor distance ---
## We bin every 5 successive scans to speed up the distance calculation
out_pois <- glm_cluster(Y,
                        family   = poisson(identity),
                        method   = "poissondist",
                        rowbins  = 5)

dim(out_pois$Y_agg)                    # 1764 scans x 4 trace-clusters
matplot(out_pois$Y_agg ^ 0.2, type = "l", lty = 1,
        xlab = "Scan index",
        ylab = "Cluster intensity ^ 0.2",
        main = paste("518 m/z traces collapsed into 4 clusters",
                     "Witten Poisson distance, rowbins = 5",
                     sep = "\n"))

##--- 2. Same with symmetrised deviance (Jensen-Shannon) ---
out_js  <- glm_cluster(Y,
                       family   = poisson(identity),
                       method   = "deviance",
                       rowbins  = 5)

dim(out_js$Y_agg)                      # 1764 scans x 5 trace-clusters
matplot(out_js$Y_agg ^ 0.2, type = "l", lty = 1,
        xlab = "Scan index",
        ylab = "Cluster intensity ^ 0.2",
        main = paste("518 m/z traces collapsed into 5 clusters",
                     "Jensen-Shannon deviance, rowbins = 5",
                     sep = "\n"))
# }
